1- Putting away the strange gods and getting rid of them. These were the small images of the pagan gods that people anciently used for good omens or to seek help. They were either the images Rachel had taken from her father and had not yet got rid of, or some images his servants may have kept during their stay in Padan-aram. This was to sanctify the heart and life for the worship of God.
2- Changing their garments and putting on new, clean clothes as a symbol of purity and cleanness of heart.

Jacob declared to those with him that this preparation was not only for moving to another place but for a holy place for the worship of God, where he would build an altar and thank God who had kept him on his way and brought him back to Bethel, and so fulfill what he had promised God in this place.

All who were with Jacob obeyed his words, and they gave him not only the images of the pagan gods but also the gold earrings they wore in their ears, because they were of the kind used in the worship of idols, since they bore the engraving of the gods. He took them all and hid them under an oak (terebinth) tree at Shechem, where they were dwelling.

If you want to worship God, you must rid yourself of your old sins through repentance, and of all the material attachments that control you, so that your heart is free for God, and you use the world only to meet your needs, and your aim is to enjoy fellowship with God.

The procession of Jacob and his family moved from Shechem toward Bethel, and God gave them awe and fear in the eyes of all their neighboring tribes, so that none of them harmed them because of what they had done to the tribe of Shechem.

If you please God and obey His commandments, He gives you favor in the eyes of those around you, so they do not harm you even if you have hidden or visible sins, for God covers you because of your repentance and your taking refuge in Him.

Jacob came to the city of Luz, which was afterward called Bethel, and built an altar to God and offered sacrifices of thanksgiving to God, who had kept him on his journey to Padan-aram and brought him back to this holy place.
Beneath Bethel: a low place in Bethel.
Allon-bachuth: that is, the oak of weeping.

Jacob used to visit his father Isaac, and Rebekah had most likely died, since she is not mentioned after his return from his uncle Laban. So he asked his father's leave and took Rebekah's nurse, who was called Deborah, to live with him as a consolation for the mother of whom he had been deprived. When they reached Bethel and had given thanks to God, Deborah died, and they buried her in a low place in Bethel under one of the trees, and wept much for her, because in that generation they honored nurses and gave them a position like that of mothers. This signifies care for those who bring up others in the Church of God, and care also for those who have departed, because Bethel, the house of God, gathers together the teachers and the children, the departed and the living. Perhaps this is the reason for mentioning Deborah's burial and the attention given to it: that the Church cares for teachers and shepherds and honors them in appreciation of their labors.

Since Jacob obeyed God and moved to Bethel, rid himself of the idols, purified himself and those with him, and then offered thanksgiving and sacrifices, God appeared to him and blessed him and confirmed to him the change of his name to Israel, that is, one who wrestles with God, so that he might begin a new, holy life with Him.

God confirmed to him the promise that his offspring would become great, and that nations would come from him and kings from his offspring would reign over them. This is what happened in the twelve tribes and the kings who reigned, such as David and Solomon.

He also promised him the inheritance of the Promised Land, that is, Canaan, as He had promised his fathers, and it is a type of the Kingdom of Heaven. Then God went up to heaven and disappeared from him.

Jacob rejoiced greatly at God's appearing to him, so he set up a pillar testifying to God's appearing to him and poured oil on it, which signifies the dedication and consecration of the place for the worship of God. He also poured out wine, which signifies joy in the worship of God and fellowship with Him. And he called the place Bethel, because God appeared there twice: the first in the dream of the ladder (ch. 28:12) and the second now in speaking with him.

entries.section: (2) The death of Rachel and the birth of Benjamin

paragraphs.text: Ephrath: it means fruitful land, and it later became Bethlehem, that is, the house of bread, where Christ was born, and it is six miles south of Jerusalem.

God graciously granted Rachel conception a second time. After they had spent a period in Bethel they moved on, seeking pasture for the flocks, and because God had assured him that he would inherit all the land of Canaan. On their way to the city of Ephrath, and a mile from it, Rachel felt the pains of childbirth, and her labor was hard and her pains severe.

entries.section: (2) The death of Rachel and the birth of Benjamin

paragraphs.text: Rachel suffered greatly in her labor, and the midwife who was helping her tried to cheer and reassure her that she would bear a son, as she had wished from God at the birth of Joseph, that He would add to her another son.

entries.section: (2) The death of Rachel and the birth of Benjamin

paragraphs.text: Ben-oni: it means son of sorrow.
Benjamin: it means son of the right hand, that is, of strength, joy and blessing.

Rachel felt that she was nearing death from the severity of the pain, so she called her son's name Ben-oni because of her great sorrow and pains, and then she died. But his father Jacob called his name Benjamin.

entries.section: (2) The death of Rachel and the birth of Benjamin

paragraphs.text: Rachel died and they buried her on the way to Ephrath, and Jacob set up a pillar on her grave to honor her, because he loved her very much. This pillar remained until this day, that is, the day Moses wrote the book, and indeed traces of this tomb are still found in Bethlehem.

Death and life are mingled together. So rejoice in every new day God gives you, and use it to prepare for the Kingdom of Heaven. That is, rejoice at the beginning of the day and remember death, and you will live above the world, enjoying fellowship with God.
Migdal Eder: the tower of the flock, which lies a mile east of Bethlehem.
Israel continued his journeys with his family, and came to Migdal Eder and pitched his tents there.

After Rachel's death, Reuben, the eldest of Israel's sons, dared to look upon Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant and his father's concubine, and desired her and lay with her. This is a great sin that neither custom nor the traditions of his time allowed, and lust was his only motive for wronging God and his father; and when Israel heard of it he was greatly grieved. Thus Reuben lost his birthright, and Joseph took it, who lived a more righteous life than the rest of his brothers, and God gave him a double portion, that is, more than the rest of his brothers (1 Chr 5:1-2).

Be in control of your desires, whether of the eye, the thought or inward longings, and drive them away by repeating the Psalms and prostrating before God, so that they do not dominate you and you fall into evil deeds and anger God. Even if you fall, hasten to repentance and to guarding your senses and thoughts, for God still loves you and is ready to rescue you from every evil.

Here is given a list of the names of the twelve sons of Israel who were born to him of his two wives and two concubines in Padan-aram. He means here that most of them, the eleven, were born at Laban's, while the last, Benjamin, was born in Canaan.

entries.section: (1) Esau's wives and children in Canaan

paragraphs.text: Three wives of Esau are mentioned here, and other lists of the names of Esau's wives are found in (ch. 26:34, ch. 28:9). Some differences in the names can be noticed, because each woman had more than one name. The first wife, Adah, is also called Bashemath; Aholibamah has another name, Judith, and her father's name is Anah, who also has another name, Beeri. The name of her grandfather Zibeon is also mentioned, to whom she is likewise ascribed as a daughter, since a granddaughter is regarded as a daughter. He is called Zibeon the Hivite, although elsewhere it says Beeri the Hittite; both belong to the Canaanite tribes, which could intermarry, for their origin is Hivite and Hittite. As for Bashemath the daughter of Ishmael, she has another name, Mahalath.
A person's name is of great value to him, so benefit from your name, if it has a special meaning, in order to live by it, for it may be a message from God to you.

entries.section: (1) Esau's wives and children in Canaan

paragraphs.text: Five sons were born to Esau in Canaan, while he was living with his father Isaac. The first was Eliphaz, by Adah, and the meaning of his name is God is his strength.
The second was Reuel, by Bashemath, and the meaning of his name is God's care.

entries.section: (1) Esau's wives and children in Canaan

paragraphs.text: Three sons were born by Aholibamah, who are:
Jeush: its meaning is God hastens.
The second, Jaalam: its meaning is God knows.
The third, Korah: its meaning is the gourd plant.
These formed tribes far from the people of God and from the faith, but many of them returned afterward to faith in Christ.

When Jacob received the blessing from his father Isaac, and Esau became sure that Jacob was the only heir of the land of Canaan, he felt that it would not hold both of them with all their possessions, so he moved south toward the mountains of Seir. It was called by this name because of its many trees, for the word Seir means thick hair. And Esau, meaning hairy, was also called Edom, meaning red, because his skin tended to redness in addition to being hairy.
The grandchildren of Esau are mentioned here: he had six grandsons by Eliphaz and four grandsons by Reuel, and his grandchildren by his three sons born of Aholibamah are not mentioned.

The sons and grandsons of Esau became dukes, that is, chiefs of tribes. It is noticeable that Korah his son by Aholibamah is mentioned a second time with his grandsons by Eliphaz, because he was related to them by marriage and shared with them in moving and in work.

Many tribes came forth from Esau, but they departed from the faith because of their distance from Jacob, and they were occupied with their many sons and possessions. Do not be preoccupied with the strength of your children and their number, or with the abundance of possessions, for all of them pass away; rather care for your faith in God and the faith of your family, which shows itself in love for God and for those around you.

Moses the prophet tells us of the rest of Jacob's life, and the most important person who appears is his son Joseph. It is mentioned here that he was seventeen years old and was helping his brothers, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, in tending the flock; perhaps Bilhah, his mother's maidservant, became like a mother to him after Rachel's death.

Joseph was the best of his brothers in his life and spiritual conduct, in his love and in his obedience to his father, while his brothers were wicked and spoke evil words about their father and about many people. So Joseph brought this evil report to his father so that he would watch over them and discipline them, and also so that he might guard against their evils. He was not proud, nor did he seek any personal gain, but wanted them to turn back from their errors, as proved by all the coming events, which will show his good feelings toward them.

Because of Joseph's distinction in love and spirituality, his father loved him and gave him a coat of many colors, a garment worn over the clothes like a cloak, worn by distinguished people and giving an appearance of greatness. The coat was an expression of Jacob's love, but at the same time it aroused his brothers' jealousy instead of moving them to imitate him. In their distress at their father's love for him, his brothers treated him harshly and spoke evil words to him that showed their hatred of him. Joseph is a type of Christ, and the coat of the Church, which He wears on His body, while the colors signify the variety of the gifts of the members of the Church.
If you see a distinguished person, try to learn a virtue from him, and keep away from jealousy and envy, which ruin your soul and corrupt your relationship with others.

A dream: dreams are either the product of what is stored in the subconscious, that is, the events that have passed through a person, which is the case with most people's dreams, or they are from God and have spiritual meanings, as in the case of Joseph. God supported Joseph with dreams so that he could bear his brothers' wrongs against him. His first dream was that he was with his brothers binding sheaves in the field, and each of them bound what he had gathered in a sheaf, and his sheaf, which he had set on the ground, arose and stood upright, while the sheaves of his brothers gathered round about it, at its feet, as if bowing down to it. When his brothers heard the divine dream, instead of ceasing their hatred of him and honoring him, since God was glorifying him, they became more distressed with him, because he would have dominion over them.
Your mother: he means Bilhah, Zilpah and Leah, who stood in the place of his mother.

Joseph saw a second dream, that the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to him. His brothers were all the more angered at him, and his father also rebuked him, but inwardly he believed in his son's standing and the glory awaiting him, and kept the matter carefully within himself.

May you understand and learn from the events around you what builds you up spiritually and binds you to God; that is, draw out God's message to you from everything you hear, so that you may grow in your spiritual life.

entries.section: (2) Jacob sends Joseph to his brothers

paragraphs.text: Joseph's ten older brothers went out to feed the flock and headed north to the region of Shechem, where they used to dwell, while Joseph and Benjamin, the young ones, their father kept with him at home because of their youth.

entries.section: (2) Jacob sends Joseph to his brothers

paragraphs.text: Jacob was anxious about his sons because of their delay in Shechem. Perhaps he feared for them from the tribes around the place, lest they take revenge on them for what they had done some time before when they killed the tribe of Shechem (ch. 34). So he asked Joseph to go and see about his brothers and ask how they were, and he obeyed at once.

Be quick in your obedience to God and to those around you, even if the request is hard or urgent, because by your obedience you show your love for others and give up your own comfort, and your standing increases, not only with them but also with God.

entries.section: (2) Jacob sends Joseph to his brothers

paragraphs.text: The vale of Hebron: the low region near the city of Hebron in the south of Canaan. Jacob sent his son Joseph to ask how his brothers were, and their flocks that they were tending.

entries.section: (2) Jacob sends Joseph to his brothers

paragraphs.text: Dothan: it means two wells, and it is nine miles northeast of Samaria and twelve miles from Shechem.

Joseph arrived, with some food, to ask about his brothers in Shechem, but he did not find them. He began to look for them left and right, and a man of that place found him wandering, and asked him what he was seeking. He told him that he was looking for his ten brothers who used to feed their flocks in that place. The man told him that he had indeed seen them, and informed him that they had gone to Dothan. So Joseph traveled until he came to Dothan and found them there.

Be persevering in your service until you complete it, however tired you are, and do not make excuses for yourself and leave the souls you serve to be lost. Care for those around you even if they wrong you, and seek the salvation and comfort of their souls, and you will win them in the end.

entries.section: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

paragraphs.text: They conspired against him: they plotted against him.

Joseph's feelings were love and concern for his brothers, but when they saw him from afar they thought among themselves how they might kill him, to be rid of his dreams and of God's blessing upon him, instead of submitting to God, honoring their brother and following his good conduct. So they agreed to kill him and cast him into one of the pits, and then lie to their father and claim that a wild beast had devoured him in the wilderness.

Sin leads to another sin after it. Jealousy led to hatred, and hatred to malice and revenge, and the last to persistence in killing and then lying. Do not be lax with the smallest sin, lest it lead you to dreadful evils, and hasten to repentance and to examining yourself day by day.

entries.section: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

paragraphs.text: Reuben the firstborn intervened to save Joseph from being killed. Perhaps he felt his responsibility before his father, when he would ask him for his brother and why he had not kept him safe. So he proposed to his brothers that they cast him into one of the dry pits, so that when they left the pit he could take him out and bring him back to his father.

entries.section: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

paragraphs.text: Joseph reached his brothers, and instead of welcoming him they fell upon him, snatched the food he had with him, and angrily stripped off his coat of many colors, and then cast him into a dry pit that was near them.

entries.section: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

paragraphs.text: Ishmaelites: that is, descendants of Ishmael, the son of Abraham; but in (v. 28) it calls them Midianites, that is, descendants of Midian, who was also a son of Abraham, by Keturah. The two tribes intermarried, and these traveling merchants resulted, so that their origin is from Ishmael and Midian.

Gilead: it lies east of the Jordan, where Laban and Jacob agreed that neither would harm the other, and they set up the heap of witness (ch. 31:48). Spicery: a kind of gum that comes from the tragacanth tree, also used in medicine.
Balm: a sweet-smelling ointment produced from the balsam plant and used in medicine and embalming.
Myrrh (ladanum): a kind of gum, also used in medicine.

After Joseph was cast into the pit, his brothers sat down to eat of the food he had brought them from their father, with an astonishing hardness of heart. And as they ate, they looked from afar and saw a caravan of merchants coming from Gilead and going to Egypt, carrying gums and sweet-smelling ointments to sell there.

entries.section: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

paragraphs.text: When Judah saw the caravan of merchants, he had compassion on Joseph and proposed to his brothers that they sell him to the caravan, so that they would be rid of him without needing to kill him, because he was their brother. Thus their hearts were softened toward him, and they agreed to his proposal.

entries.section: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

paragraphs.text: They drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold him to the merchants for twenty pieces of silver. Twenty pieces of silver: that is, twenty shekels, and the shekel is about 15 grams.

entries.section: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

paragraphs.text: Reuben had gone far away to do some work while they were eating and selling their brother to the merchants. When he came back, he looked for him in the pit and did not find him, and he was troubled and asked them about him. They told him what they had done, and he was deeply grieved and said to them, What shall I say to my father? That is, I have no answer or explanation for Joseph's disappearance.
Kid: a male goat.

Joseph's brothers hid their crime by killing a kid of the goats and staining Joseph's coat with its blood, and they sent it, by one of the servants or one of themselves, to their father, telling him that they had found this coat in the wilderness and asking him to determine whether it was Joseph's coat or not, intending to make their father believe that Joseph was dead.
If you sin, repent of your sin so that God may forgive it, and do not persist in it and try to hide it with other sins such as lying, lest you anger God and stir up people against you.
Sackcloth: a coarse black cloth made of goat's hair.

Loins: the sides of his thighs. The meaning is that the sackcloth was worn from the waist and hung down over the sides of the thighs. When Jacob examined the coat, he was certain that it was Joseph's, and understood from the blood that a wild beast had devoured him in the wilderness. So he wept much for him and rent his clothes, an ancient and well-known sign of great grief, and put on coarse cloth, which is sackcloth, as a sign of abasement. His sons and daughters tried to calm his grief but could not; rather he said, I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Hades, or the abyss, was the meeting place of all the departed, because Christ had not yet accomplished redemption.
Potiphar: a name connected with Ra, the sun god.

Officer (eunuch): either he was in fact one of the eunuchs, or, according to another opinion, it had become a title given to those of high rank in the service of the king of Egypt. So either he was a eunuch and had a wife who lived with him as a sister, or he was an ordinary married man and this was merely a title for him.
Pharaoh: most probably one of the kings of the fifteenth or sixteenth dynasty, and most probably one of the Hyksos, who occupied some places in Egypt and are called the Shepherd Kings.
Captain of the guard: the one responsible for security in Egypt, like a minister of the interior, and also responsible for the prisons.
The merchants reached Egypt and sold their goods and the slaves they had with them, and Potiphar bought Joseph to be a servant to him.
We notice in this chapter that Joseph is a type of Christ in many respects, which will be gathered at the end of chapter fifty.
Judah and Tamar

An Adullamite: from the city of Adullam, one of the great cities of Canaan, lying near Bethlehem. Judah the son of Jacob went to visit a person who seems to have been his friend, called Hirah, a pagan man who lived in one of the cities of Canaan called Adullam.

While Judah was in the city of Adullam, where he stayed a while in the house of his friend Hirah, his eyes wandered and he was taken with a girl, and his desire was stirred toward her, and he married her although she was a pagan, the daughter of a man named Shuah.

Beware of mixing with those far from God and of leaving your senses lax, lest they draw you into a conduct and life far from God. If you become bound to lusts, your way to repentance becomes harder than before. Do not cling to sin and grow accustomed to it, lest you sell your Christ and then regret it afterward when you have become weak.
This pagan woman bore Judah three sons, Er and Onan, and after some years he went to the city of Chezib, which lies in the south of Palestine, and she bore a third son, whom she called Shelah.

Judah was preoccupied with and delighted in lust and in having many sons, and of course he lived several years among the pagans and was affected by their ways. He did not know that all he had done was vanity, distancing him from God, since his last son was born in Chezib, whose meaning is lie. This signifies that all he had obtained of sons and lust was a lie and without value; yet God turns our vain works into the greatest thing, since Christ humbled Himself and came from the offspring of Judah and of Tamar the pagan, who will be mentioned shortly.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Judah's two sons

paragraphs.text: Judah was still living among the pagans, and his firstborn son Er grew up, so he gave him a pagan girl called Tamar. But the character of his son Er was wicked, because his mother was a pagan and he lived among wicked pagans. God gave him the chance to learn faith from his father and to live with God, but he persisted in evil and died while young.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Judah's two sons

paragraphs.text: Judah asked his second son Onan to marry Tamar, the wife of his brother Er who had died, so that he might raise up offspring to his brother and then to himself. For it was the custom in that time that if a brother died without children, his brother married his wife, and the firstborn son was counted as the son of the dead man so that his name would not be blotted out, while the sons after him were counted to the living husband. The Law of Moses later laid this down (Deut 25:5), all in expectation of the Messiah, the Savior. This has no meaning now after the coming of the Messiah, for Christianity forbids the marriage of a brother to the wife of his dead brother, because she is regarded as his sister, and what matters now is spiritual virtues and preparation for eternity, not the begetting of children.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Judah's two sons

paragraphs.text: Onan was selfish and loved money, though he was a young man, as a result of his wicked upbringing. He did not want the inheritance to be shared by three brothers, but to be for himself and for Shelah his young brother only, so he did not want to beget children by Tamar. So when he was joined to her bodily, he took care that this should not lead to a complete relationship and the begetting of offspring. God was angry with him because of his persistence in evil and greed, and he died also.

Do not be attached to money and passing material things, lest they gain control over you and lead you to wicked deeds, so that you provoke God's anger and lose every blessing in your life, and grieve in your worldly life and in the life to come.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Judah's two sons

paragraphs.text: His daughter-in-law: his son's wife.

Judah did not take heed of his sin in clinging to the wicked and begetting wicked sons, and he was still thinking of material fruits, that is, having offspring called by his name from his sons. But there was no small difference in age between Onan and Shelah; that is, Shelah was a child who could not marry. So Judah told his daughter-in-law Tamar to remain in her father's house until Shelah grew up, and he would give her to him. But in truth fear had begun to control him about Shelah's death, for some people, by a mistaken belief, suppose that a wife may sometimes be the cause of trouble to whomever she marries, because of their pagan beliefs in bad luck, omens and pessimism. So he feared for his son's death, and perhaps he wanted to save him from it and keep him away from marrying Tamar; that is, he was lying in his promise to Tamar to give her to Shelah.

Judah's mind was polluted by evil and by the thoughts of the pagans. So be careful in what you see or hear and in all your relationships, and do not promise anything you cannot guarantee; rather let your heart be pure and your promises true, and you will receive God's blessing.

The Canaanite woman, Judah's wife, the daughter of Shuah, died, and after the mourning Judah's heart was comforted, and he went up to a town called Timnath, lying west of Jerusalem, where he had sheep. The season of sheep-shearing came, so he went to oversee the shearers, and Tamar his daughter-in-law heard that he was going to Timnath.

Tamar was troubled because Judah had not fulfilled his promise to give her his son Shelah as a husband, although he had grown up, in order to raise up offspring to her dead husband Er. She was, like any woman, hoping that the Messiah, the Savior, would come from her offspring, as God had promised Eve and then Abraham.

So she thought of a ruse to raise up offspring for herself. She put off her widow's garments, which were most likely dark or black, and put on bright clothes, covered her face with a veil, and sat on the road to the city of Timnath, where Judah would pass, in a place called Enaim, whose meaning is two eyes. Her appearance was like that of a professional harlot, of those who devote themselves to fornication to please the goddess Ashtoreth, and who cover their faces and wait on the roads to commit fornication with whoever passes by them. And Judah indeed passed by on the road and saw her, and understood that she was one of the harlots, and did not know that she was his daughter-in-law, because her face was covered.

Lust was stirred in Judah's heart, so he asked Tamar, not knowing her, to lie with him. She asked him for payment, as one of the professional harlots, and he promised to give her a kid. She asked him to give her a pledge, that is, a guarantee or proof that he would fulfill the promise. He said to her, What pledge shall I give you? She asked for his signet, and his bracelets, a piece of cloth wound around the head like a turban, and also his staff. He gave her what she asked, and lay with her, and she conceived. Afterward she returned and put on her widow's garments and lived in her house.

We must not fail to add here that whatever Tamar's motive or grief, a spiritual person must never resort to a wrong way to attain a lawful or noble end. A sound goal must be reached by a sound way, and it would have been better for Tamar to pray and believe in God, who is able to do her justice.
Let her take it to her: she is responsible for not taking her payment, that is, the kid, and let her take for herself the pledge that he left with her.
We shall be shamed: so that no one may shame us for not having paid the wages.

After Judah went to Timnath, he sent the kid by his friend the Adullamite to Enaim to give the harlot her payment, but he did not find her. He asked about her, and the people of the place denied that there was a harlot who used to sit there. So he returned with the kid to Judah, who said, Let her take the pledge to her, and I am not responsible, and I have not failed to give her the payment.

After three months the signs of pregnancy began to appear on Tamar, and when her neighbors learned of it they were very troubled and told her father-in-law Judah, who was angry and decided that she should die by burning with fire, and he came to carry out the sentence of death upon her. When they brought her out to be burned, she said to Judah before those gathered, Whose are these? By the man whose these are, am I with child. And she brought out the pledge, that is, the signet, the bracelets and the staff. When Judah looked at her he was ashamed of himself, and declared before the people of the city that she was innocent, indeed more righteous than he, because he had failed in his promise and had not given her his son Shelah, and he was responsible for her, because he was the one who had lain with her. So he took her to his house, to be a wife to him, and moreover to keep her and support her and the one in her womb. And the chastity of this woman appeared before all, for she did not seek her lust but only the begetting of offspring, so she lay with this old man.

Do not be hasty in judging others, lest they be more righteous than you. Do not judge, that you be not judged, and try to make excuses however clear and great the faults are. At least say to yourself that all people are weak, and pray for all, or at least pray for yourself, for you may be weaker than they.
After Potiphar bought Joseph as a slave from the Ishmaelites, he worked in his house faithfully and God blessed him, so his success and his distinction from the rest of the slaves appeared.

God's work with you shines out in affliction. When Jacob was fleeing from Esau he saw the ladder reaching to heaven; when Laban pursued him God appeared to him; and when Joseph was sold as a slave God gave him more success than all those around him. So do not be disturbed by afflictions, but seek God's help, and He will make you feel His presence with you, will gladden you, and will turn the affliction into a blessing.

God gave Joseph favor in Potiphar's eyes, and he admired his faithfulness, devotion and success and trusted him, so that he raised him above all the slaves and made him overseer not only over his house but over all his possessions, fields and lands, and Joseph managed them with energy and success.

God's blessing on Joseph increased, and He made him a blessing to those around him, that is, to Potiphar's house. His possessions increased and his affairs prospered at Joseph's hand, which made his heart cling to Joseph.

Besides his success and energy, Joseph was also distinguished by his good looks. Such was Potiphar's trust in him that he no longer supervised him but left him to manage the house and all the possessions in complete freedom, and Potiphar asked of him only his necessary needs, such as food.

Joseph accepted to work faithfully as a slave and did not murmur, although his father and grandfathers were rich and of great standing. So accept hard circumstances and lowly work for God's sake, and know that greatness is within you and not in your outward appearance, for your strength springs from God's dwelling in you.

Potiphar's wife was taken with Joseph's good looks, his energy, his wisdom and the strength of his personality, evident in his management of the house and all the possessions, and she desired him emotionally and physically. If her husband was truly a eunuch and not merely in title, that would be a greater motive for her to desire Joseph.

Joseph answered firmly and respectfully this woman who desired to commit adultery with him, and tried to persuade her to give up her desire because of her husband's favors to him, for he had raised him above all the slaves and entrusted to him all his possessions except his wife. Then he gave another reason for refusing adultery, which was that God sees him and he cannot anger Him by this very wicked deed.

If you always see God before your eyes, this will keep you from every sin, for if you feel His presence you will fear Him and submit to Him; and if you do sin, you will hasten to repent at His feet, and He will forgive you, raise you up and fortify you with His power.

Potiphar's wife did not despair, and she tried every day, in different ways, to entice Joseph in order to make him fall into adultery, but he kept refusing in every way and fleeing from her, relying on God's power, and she could not weaken him.
About this time: the time when Joseph used to enter the house every day to do his work.

This woman, in her cunning, arranged to send all the servants and maids out to tasks around the house, so that when Joseph entered to do his daily work there was no one in the house but her. She approached him to persuade him that the place was empty and that it was easy to lie with her, but he refused firmly. Then she tried to compel him by force and authority, and his firmness in refusing only increased, so she was enraged because her pride was wounded. She fell upon him in a last attempt to weaken him by clinging to him, and caught hold of his garment. But the most important thing to him was not to fall into sin, so he left his garment in her hand, which may have been torn in his struggle with her, and was forced to flee from the house naked. He cared for nothing but keeping his purity, sacrificing not only his reputation but risking being seized and thrown into prison, or even put to death.

Flee for your life from evil whatever the cost, for the salvation of your soul is more important than any loss. Do not mind what people say, and keep yourself pure even if you are accused of the most terrible crimes, and in this way you keep God's good pleasure toward you.

When Joseph fled, Potiphar's wife was enraged because he had shattered her pride and her burning lust by his insistence on purity. She cried out with a loud voice until her servants and maids gathered round her, and claimed that Joseph had tried to toy with her and assault her, and had taken off his clothes, and when she refused and cried out he was afraid and fled out of the house naked, and there was his garment in her hands before them as clear evidence of the accusation.

Potiphar's wife continued in her deception, and when her husband came from his work she falsely accused Joseph of having tried to assault her, saying that he took off his clothes and when she cried out he was forced to flee naked. And of course she played the weak one before him, with weeping and a sense of being wronged, to hide the evil within her.

This wicked woman stirred up her husband's feelings and manhood against Joseph, and he was very angry and decided at once to throw him into the very harsh prison, which was the prison of those who offended against the king, which was under Potiphar's supervision and authority and was most likely near his palace. It is said that its place was north of the pyramid of Saqqara and it is still called Joseph's prison to this day.

Do not judge matters hastily, especially if you have fallen into anger, for your anger robs you of much of your wisdom and understanding. Wait, even a little, until you calm down, and seek God's help, and He will support and guide you.

Joseph was thrown into prison and irons were put on his feet and hands, and they treated him harshly like the other criminals imprisoned there, as the Psalm declares (Ps 105:18). But God gave him favor in the eyes of the jailers and those in charge of the prison, for they noticed his gentleness and his words and good conduct, so they began to treat him kindly and then trusted him so much that they let him help them in the work of the prison and the care of the prisoners. He became like an official in the prison, and his faithfulness and energy appeared so that the officer in charge of the prison entrusted to him the running of the prison, and he managed everything in it.

This change in treatment was certainly with the knowledge of Potiphar, who supervised the prison near his house. This means that he reconsidered, and began to regain his confidence in Joseph and to direct the accusation in his heart toward his wife. But he could not release Joseph from prison, or his dignity would be exposed to insult because of his wife's wicked lust. Some opinions hold that his wife may have been related to the king, so he refrained from taking any decision against her; or that if he divorced her she might take a large part of his possessions, so he left things as they were and was content to agree to Joseph's being honored inside the prison.
Joseph in prison

entries.section: (1) The butler and the baker in prison

paragraphs.text: Two of the chief officials in Pharaoh's palace were accused. One was the king's cupbearer (butler), responsible for all the drinks served to Pharaoh and all those in his palace, and the other was the baker, responsible for the foods of pastries and doughs served to the king and all his attendants. They were eunuchs, either in fact, because of their responsibility inside the palace for the king and all his women, or it was merely a title for these two offices. This accusation was probably taking part in a plot to kill the king, so he was angry with them and ordered them thrown into prison, and they put them in the king's prison attached to Potiphar's house, where Joseph was imprisoned.

entries.section: (1) The butler and the baker in prison

paragraphs.text: The man in charge of the prison cared for the butler and the baker because of their high standing with Pharaoh, which might return at any time if he forgave them, and he found no one better than Joseph to take care of them. They remained for a time in prison, which gave an opportunity for friendship and a relationship between Joseph and them.

If you please God, He will give you favor in the eyes of people, and in proportion to your faithfulness and energy He makes people trust you. So do not murmur at the abundance of work and responsibilities, but seek God's help, and He will give you strength, wisdom and success.

entries.section: (2) The dreams of the butler and the baker

paragraphs.text: Sad: troubled and grieved.
There is no interpreter of it: that is, no one to interpret it.

God allowed Pharaoh's two eunuchs to dream two dreams while they were in prison, for Joseph to interpret, so that this would later be a means of his rising to the throne of Egypt. When they woke they were perplexed, because they did not understand the interpretation of their dreams. When Joseph came in to them in the morning to oversee their service and their needs, he noticed their sadness and asked them the reason, and they told him it was because of strange dreams they had dreamed the night before. He reassured them, and this shows Joseph's kindness and love, since he cared for the prisoners and their feelings, and his work was not merely the performing of a job; everything he did was a free service which he was not bound to perform, but he carried it out with complete faithfulness for God's sake.

Then Joseph's humility appeared in his ascribing the wisdom and power to God, who is able to interpret the two dreams and who would give him this understanding, because in this time magicians and soothsayers who interpret dreams had multiplied in Egypt, but with the help of Satan and not by the power of God. Joseph's humility shows that he is a son of God, who works with him and through him.

Always give glory to God in everything you succeed in or do, and thank Him in your prayers and before people, for He is the source of grace and power in all you accomplish, and He will bless you and pour out on you more abundant blessings.

entries.section: (2) The dreams of the butler and the baker

paragraphs.text: Branches: shoots.
Brought forth ripe grapes: ripened.

The king's cupbearer told Joseph his dream: that he saw a vine with three branches, which ripened, and he saw its blossoms and the clusters of grapes hanging from it. He took some of the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, which was in his hand, and gave it to him.

entries.section: (2) The dreams of the butler and the baker

paragraphs.text: Joseph interpreted the dream: the three branches are three days, after which Pharaoh would bring him out of prison and restore him to his former office and position. Perhaps he had discovered his innocence, and he would again oversee the king's drinks.

entries.section: (2) The dreams of the butler and the baker

paragraphs.text: Joseph clung to the hope of leaving prison, so he asked the king's cupbearer to intercede for him with Pharaoh to bring him out, especially since he deserved this for the following reasons:
1- That he was a free man who had been stolen from the land of the Hebrews and sold as a slave, so that he might return to his former freedom and dignity.
2- That he had done nothing in Egypt to deserve being thrown into prison.
Several things appear from Joseph's words, which are:
1- His mistake in relying on human beings and not on God, and therefore God allowed the cupbearer to forget him, that he might learn to depend on God alone.

2- Joseph's kindness in not accusing his brothers of treachery and of selling him to the merchants, but covering for them, for he said that he was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews; likewise he did not accuse Potiphar's wife of wicked lust and lying, but said that he had done nothing wrong.
Be gentle in your speech about others or with them, and do not hasten to blame, but cover their faults when you explain any matter, and consider everyone's feelings with love.

entries.section: (2) The dreams of the butler and the baker

paragraphs.text: White: that is, the fine flour from which Pharaoh's pastries are made, also called fine flour (semolina). The chief baker took courage when he saw Joseph's ability to interpret dreams, and told him his dream also, in which he saw himself carrying on his head three baskets, and in the uppermost basket were various pastries and baked goods for Pharaoh, and then the birds of the air came and ate them.

entries.section: (2) The dreams of the butler and the baker

paragraphs.text: Joseph interpreted the dream: the three baskets are three days, after which Pharaoh would command that he be killed. Perhaps he had discovered his responsibility for the accusation made against him, and after his death his body would be hanged on a tree and the birds of the air would eat it.

entries.section: (3) The fulfillment of the two dreams

paragraphs.text: Lifted up the head: announced his judgment and decision.

Pharaoh made a great feast for all his servants on the occasion of his birthday, and took the opportunity to announce his judgment in the matter of two of the chief of those who worked for him, the chief butler and the chief baker, whom he had thrown into prison some time before so that he might examine the accusations made against them.

entries.section: (3) The fulfillment of the two dreams

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh decided to restore the chief butler to his office, but he ordered the chief baker killed and his body hanged on a tree, as Joseph had interpreted the two dreams.

entries.section: (3) The fulfillment of the two dreams

paragraphs.text: God allowed the chief butler to forget Joseph's matter, since he was occupied with the celebrations and the joy of his return to his post. This was, of course, ingratitude toward Joseph for his care of him the whole time he was in prison, and for interpreting his troubling dream and reassuring him; but God allowed it so that Joseph might learn to depend on Him alone.

Do not be distressed at people's selfishness and their preoccupation with their own interests at the expense of yours, and trust that God, who allowed it, will turn it to your good and lead you to depend on Him and to test Him in your life. Know that God's work and help are far better than the service of human beings and their help to you.
Joseph on the throne of Egypt
Fed: from feeding, that is, they ate and drank and were satisfied.
Meadow: a place full of grass and plants that animals can eat.

Two years passed after the chief butler left prison and returned to his post in Pharaoh's palace, and Joseph was entirely forgotten and occupied himself with his work. But God, who does not forget His children, allowed Pharaoh to see a dream in which he saw himself standing by a river, most likely meaning the Nile, and he saw seven well-favored kine, fat-fleshed, come up out of the river and go about in a meadow, where they fed and were satisfied as they wished. Then, after that, seven very lean and ill-favored kine came up out of the river and fell upon the seven fat kine and ate them up. Then Pharaoh awoke from his sleep, troubled.

Your God who orders your life moves the whole world for your sake. He troubles others or gives them blessings so that He may keep you safe in the end, bless your life and move everyone to serve you, even if they are the greatest of people or rulers. So do not be disturbed by your weakness or the pressures that pass over you, even if all people rise against you, for you are kept in the hands of God, who is loving and able to do all things.
Blasted: dry and scorched.
East wind: the khamsin winds that blow on Egypt from the southeast, hot and laden with dust.

Pharaoh slept that same night and dreamed a second, strange dream, in which he saw a stalk of grain bearing seven ears full of large kernels, and good to look at. Then he saw behind it another stalk bearing seven ears very dry, indeed scorched by the hot east wind, and he noticed that they leaned over the full ears and swallowed them up. Then Pharaoh woke from his dream.

Pharaoh could not sleep after that and remained troubled until morning. So he sent and called for all the wise men and magicians for whom Egypt was famous for their knowledge of interpreting dreams, to interpret his two dreams for him, but they were all unable to do so.

entries.section: (2) Joseph is brought out of prison

paragraphs.text: When all the wise men were unable to interpret Pharaoh's dreams, the chief butler remembered his fault toward Joseph, for he had forgotten him for two years, so he hastened to Pharaoh and confessed his fault against Joseph.

When you remember any sin, hasten to repent of it and try to repair what can be repaired, and know that God rejoices at your return even after many years. Do not be ashamed to make right your sin before people, for the salvation of your soul is more important than anything. Do not be content with confession before the priest, but also repair, as far as you can, what you have spoiled, under the guidance of your spiritual father.

entries.section: (2) Joseph is brought out of prison

paragraphs.text: The chief butler told Pharaoh what had happened to him in prison, he and the chief baker, and how they dreamed in one night and were troubled by their dreams, and how Joseph interpreted them for them, and it happened exactly as he told them.

entries.section: (2) Joseph is brought out of prison

paragraphs.text: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace: God will make the dreams for Pharaoh's good.

They hastened to bring Joseph out of the prison, and he shaved and changed his prison clothes for clothes fit for meeting the king. When he came before him, Pharaoh said to him, I have dreamed a dream, and there is none that can interpret it, and I have heard say of you that you can understand a dream. Joseph turned the glory to God, who gives him the ability to interpret. Joseph is a type of Christ in His incarnation and redemption: as Joseph was cast into prison and bonds, so Christ bore the bonds of our sins and was crucified for us. And in Joseph's rising to the throne of Egypt he is a type of Christ, who rose to raise us in Him and change our life as he changed his garments.

entries.section: (3) The interpretation of the two dreams

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh told his two dreams to Joseph and made clear in them that the seven lean and ill-favored kine had eaten up the fat kine and it could not be known that they had eaten them, but they remained as lean and ill-favored as before; and likewise the seven dry ears swallowed up the fat ones and remained as dry as they were.

entries.section: (3) The interpretation of the two dreams

paragraphs.text: Joseph interpreted the two dreams: the seven fat kine and the seven full ears are seven years of plenty and abundant good that would come on Egypt, and after them would follow seven years of famine, which are signified by the seven lean kine and the seven thin ears. The repetition of the dream was to confirm the meaning and that it would shortly come to pass. In a tactful and gentle way he announced to Pharaoh the one God, who gave him these dreams and sent him their interpretation to warn him so that he might order his affairs, for Pharaoh believed in many pagan gods and did not know the one God.
In your speech with others you can present your God without an explicit proclamation, for He will appear in your love, your faith and your trust in Him, and all will feel the living Christ in you.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: Joseph was not content with interpreting the dreams, but also offered a solution to the problem and counsel for managing the affairs of Egypt, which included the following:
1- Choosing a wise man to store up wheat in the years of plenty for the people and the animals to eat in the years of famine.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: 2- This wise ruler would be helped by a group of overseers over all the land of Egypt to gather from it one fifth of the produce of the land for Pharaoh, since formerly they used to gather a tenth for Pharaoh, but now, because the harvest would be abundant, they could gather a fifth.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: 3- He would build storehouses in all the cities of Egypt in which this produce would be gathered from the cities and the villages around them throughout the years of plenty, so that the land would be kept from perishing by hunger in the years of famine.

When you notice any problem, do not be content with knowing it or fall into condemning the one who caused it, but offer the solution if you can, and if you do not know a solution, be silent and pray until God intervenes.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh and all his servants, his counselors around him, were impressed not only with the interpretation of the dreams but with the orderly solution Joseph offered to the problem.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh asked his servants, Can we find such a one as this, a man wise like Joseph? All showed their admiration for him, and he decided before everyone that he was the wise man he had chosen to be ruler and manager of Egypt.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: According to your word shall all my people be ruled (literally, at your mouth shall all my people kiss): an expression of the whole people's submission to him, not in the literal sense.
Pharaoh gave Joseph authority over the royal palace and decreed that all should submit to him.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: His ring: the king's signet ring, which he wears on his hand and with which he seals all commands so that they are authoritative. Vestures of fine linen: garments of white linen worn by priests and the great.
A gold chain: a sign of greatness and honor.
He made him to ride in the second chariot: that is, the place second after the king directly.
The king confirmed his decision to make Joseph ruler over Egypt in five ways:
1- He gave him his ring to seal with it the decrees issued by the king for all Egypt.
2- He arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, which the great men of the kingdom wear.
3- He put a gold chain about his neck, a sign of great honor.
4- He gave him the second chariot in the kingdom, proclaiming that he was in the place second after the king directly.
5- The submission of all the people to him, and his command to them to bow the knee before him as he passed among them.

entries.section: (4) Joseph's counsel and his appointment as ruler of Egypt

paragraphs.text: Zaphnath-paaneah: an ancient Egyptian word meaning food of life.
Asenath: connected with the goddess of wisdom.
Potipherah: connected with Ra, the sun god.
On: that is, the city of the sun, which is now located in the area of Matariya and Ain Shams.

Pharaoh gave Joseph a new name as a proclamation of his new position as ruler of Egypt, and gave him in marriage the daughter of a priest, because priests held a very high place in Egypt at that time. He was thirty years old when he became ruler in Egypt, and then he went out from Pharaoh's palace to carry out his duties as ruler of Egypt and manage its affairs, because the years of plenty were about to begin.

entries.section: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

paragraphs.text: By handfuls: abundantly.
All the food: the fifth of the produce that they gave to Pharaoh.

The seven years of plenty began and the harvest was abundant, and the overseers under Joseph gathered the fifth of the produce of the land, which they gave as a due to Pharaoh, and stored it in the storehouses Joseph built in the cities for all that was gathered from the surrounding villages. This was a successful administrative system to make storage easy and the later sale of the grain to the people, to reduce transport costs and to make things easy for the people, for he did not set up the storehouses in the capital but spread them in all the cities, and thereby involved many overseers in the responsibility so that each one would be accountable for his work.

entries.section: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

paragraphs.text: The overseers began at first to write down the quantities of grain they gathered, but the quantity of grain increased until they were unable to write it down because of its great abundance, which he compared to the sand of the sea in its multitude.

entries.section: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

paragraphs.text: During the years of plenty Asenath bore Joseph two sons. The first he called Manasseh, which means causing to forget, because God made him forget all the hardships of slavery and prison in Egypt, and also the hardships he met from his brothers when he was in his father's house.

entries.section: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

paragraphs.text: His second son he called Ephraim, which means doubly fruitful, because God gave him success and wealth in Egypt after he had tasted the humiliation of slavery and prison there.

entries.section: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

paragraphs.text: The seven years of plenty ended and the famine began, not only in Egypt but in the surrounding lands such as Palestine. All lands means the whole region around Egypt, and this may have been because of the scarcity of rain in all the lands, which also feeds the Nile. So the people began to suffer from hunger for lack of food, but in Egypt there was stored grain.

entries.section: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

paragraphs.text: The people in Egypt were distressed by hunger and complained to Pharaoh, who sent them to Joseph, and he began to sell them food from the stored grain.

entries.section: (5) The years of plenty and the beginning of the famine

paragraphs.text: People came from the lands around Egypt when they heard that there was food in Egypt, and began to buy grain from its storehouses.

Be wise, and store up good works and holy worship in the days of your strength, that is, your youth, and in every time you have the ability to work, that is, throughout your life, so that if your health and ability weaken, your thoughts will have been filled with spiritual things, and you will enjoy the store within you and never hunger, by the grace of God dwelling in you. Joseph's brothers in Egypt

entries.section: (1) Jacob's illness and his blessing of Joseph

paragraphs.text: Joseph heard of his father's illness and felt that it might be his final illness, so he hurried with his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, so that Jacob might bless them before his death. When Jacob learned that Joseph had come, he strengthened himself despite his weakness and sat up on his bed.

entries.section: (1) Jacob's illness and his blessing of Joseph

paragraphs.text: An everlasting possession: not only for the descendants of Jacob in Canaan, but because Canaan is a symbol of the Kingdom of Heaven, which is inherited by those who believe in Christ, who is of the seed of Jacob. The possession is not limited to the earthly possession that was fulfilled in the Old Testament, but it is a symbol of the heavenly possession that is fulfilled in the New Testament. Jacob declared to Joseph that God had appeared to him at Luz, which was later called Bethel, when he was fleeing from the face of Esau, and then a second time when he returned from his uncle Laban, and that He blessed him and promised him numerous offspring and the inheritance of the land of Canaan. So he declares to him that the blessing he would give to him and to his children is from God, the source of blessings. In the same way, the Church blesses her children by the Holy Spirit who dwells in her.

Enjoy the blessings of the Church through the prayers and the Holy Sacraments, so that you may become a source of blessing to everyone you meet and every place you go to, and so be the light of the world and the salt of the earth.

entries.section: (1) Jacob's illness and his blessing of Joseph

paragraphs.text: Jacob gave Joseph's blessing two portions instead of the one portion that he gave to each of his brothers, because of his love and Joseph's distinction in forgiveness and giving. In this way Joseph became the firstborn (1 Chr 5:1) in place of Reuben, who lost his birthright by lying with his father's wife (ch. 35:21-26). So the two sons of Joseph are in their inheritance like the rest of Joseph's brothers in the inheritance. As for the children whom God would give to Joseph after Ephraim and Manasseh, they would inherit in the Promised Land following their brothers Ephraim and Manasseh; that is, they would have no third portion, because Joseph's portion became the two portions of Ephraim and Manasseh.

entries.section: (1) Jacob's illness and his blessing of Joseph

paragraphs.text: As Jacob was blessing Joseph, he remembered Joseph's mother Rachel, whom he loved very much and whom he had buried beside Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. He did so to bind the heart of his son Joseph to the Land of Promise, Canaan, so that he would feel that he was a stranger in the land of Egypt, even though he ruled over it.

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Jacob's eyes were dim with age, so he asked Joseph about the two men who were with him. Joseph was then 56 years old, while Ephraim and Manasseh were young men in their early twenties. Joseph said to him that they were his sons whom God had given him in Egypt, and then he brought them near to his father, who embraced them and kissed them.

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Jacob declared his joy at seeing and embracing Joseph's two sons, and said to him, "I had hoped to see you, and God has granted me not only to see you but your children also." When Joseph took the two grandsons out from between Jacob's knees and arms, for he had been holding them close, rejoicing at meeting them, the two grandsons then bowed down to their grandfather out of respect and reverence. The word "bowed" appears in the Septuagint as "they bowed down."

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Joseph brought his two sons near, Manasseh the firstborn at Jacob's right hand and Ephraim the younger at his left, so that the greater blessing would be given to the firstborn. But God had made known to Jacob that the younger would be a greater blessing than the firstborn, so he laid his right hand on Ephraim and his left on Manasseh. In this way his hands formed the shape of a cross, a symbol of all the blessings of the New Testament that come through the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Jacob blessed Joseph's two sons with the following blessings:
1- The blessing of the God who shepherded him and his fathers: He will shepherd them with His care.

2- The blessing of the God who delivered him by His angel from many afflictions, such as his exposure to being killed by Esau, then Laban's exploitation and pursuit of him, and his protection from the surrounding tribes after the killing of the tribe of Shechem: He blesses the two grandsons and delivers them from every affliction.
3- They will receive the blessing of the name of their grandfather Jacob and of his fathers Isaac and Abraham, when they inherit the Promised Land as God promised.
4- The blessing of numerous offspring.

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Joseph was displeased that the greater blessing was given to the younger Ephraim, and he thought that this was because of the weakness of his father Jacob's eyesight. So he tried to move his father's right hand from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's, and said to him that Manasseh was the firstborn. Jacob answered him, "God has made known to me that Manasseh will be blessed, but his younger brother will be more fruitful and a greater blessing than his brother." This indeed happened, as appears from the history of the people of Ephraim in the following:
1- Great men came from him, such as Joshua the son of Nun and Samuel the prophet.
2- His number was large. In the first census taken in the days of Moses, the number of those enrolled for war from Ephraim was 40,500, while that of Manasseh was 32,200 (Num 1:32-35).
3- Shiloh, where the tabernacle of meeting was set up for a period of time, was one of the cities of Ephraim (1 Sam 1:3).

4- The tribe of Manasseh was divided in its dwelling: half of it lived east of the Jordan River and mixed with the idolaters, while the other half lived west of it, which led to the weakening of the tribe.

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Jacob blessed Joseph's two sons, and they became a blessing, so much so that they were used as a byword for blessing, and it would be said, "God bless you like Ephraim and Manasseh." He put Ephraim before Manasseh because he would become a greater blessing, and the kingdom of Israel was sometimes called Ephraim because of the greatness of the tribe of Ephraim.

God gives His blessing to the great or the small, so be strong, believe in God, and ask for His help and blessing, however small, despised or neglected you may be, for by God's blessing and your faith you will become great.

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Before he died, Jacob assured his son Joseph of God's promise to give them the land of Canaan, and that He would bring them back to it from Egypt so that they might inherit it.

entries.section: (2) Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

paragraphs.text: He told Joseph that he had given him a portion (a share) greater than that of his brothers, as he had said before that he had made an inheritance for Ephraim and Manasseh like the rest of Joseph's brothers. Here he adds a new piece of information: that he had taken some land from the Amorites, not only the plot that he had bought from Hamor, the father of Shechem, but it may be that some of the Amorites had attacked his plot of land there, so he fought them, recovered his land, and took some of their neighboring lands. He gave the land and the well that was in it to Joseph, as is mentioned in (Jn 4:5, 6). Jacob's blessing of his sons
In the last days: that is, the future.
Jacob called his twelve sons to give them his farewell charges before he died, and to bless them and prophesy to them about their future.
My might and the beginning of my strength: the firstborn represents strength and blessing.
Excellency: the best.

The excellency of dignity and the excellency of power: the firstborn is expected to lift up his father's head by his good conduct and distinction. Jacob praises his son Reuben, whose name means "son of the vision," saying that he was expected to represent the greatness and loftiness of his father, and that in him were the fullness of blessing and strength. So it is a rebuke within the manner of a commendation.

Be gentle in rebuking others and praise them with kind words, so that you convey to them the meaning you intend, which is that they leave their sins and walk uprightly, without wounding their feelings.
Boiling over like water: unstable; you rise like water that boils with its bubbles, then cools and sinks. You shall not excel: you have no preeminence over your brothers.
Simeon and Levi are brothers: Simeon is the forefather of the scribes and Levi the forefather of the priests.

Jacob continued his rebuke of Reuben, but in more direct words, since he blamed him for his instability, like water that boils over and then cools, and for losing preeminence over his brothers because he fell into a shameful sin, which was his lying with his father's concubine Bilhah.
Weapons of injustice are their swords: their wrong against the tribe of Shechem, all of whose men they killed because of the sin of one person, Shechem.
Let my soul not enter: I cannot sit between them, because of their anger and their evil.
Let not my honor be united: my soul would be humbled and I would be without honor if I sat among them, because of their great evil. They killed a man: Shechem and his tribe.
In their consent: when they pretended gentleness and agreement with Hamor and Shechem, they deceived them.
They hamstrung an ox: they struck it at the bottom of its leg near the foot, so that it fell, and they killed it. The ox symbolizes the strong man, that is, Shechem and the men of his tribe.

The brothers Simeon and Levi were united in the anger and vengeance that appeared in their killing of the men of the tribe of Shechem (ch. 34). Therefore Jacob, the man of God, declares that he finds no rest in associating with them, because of their dreadful evil and their fury that knows no limit.

Jacob denounces their anger and vengeance because it is severe and cruel, and God's punishment for them is that they will be scattered in their inheritance among the tribes of Israel and will not have a unified territory. The tribe of Simeon gradually dwindled, as appears from the two censuses taken by Moses (Num 1, 26), and when they entered the Promised Land under Joshua they had no portion of their own, but possessed some parts of the land of Judah (Josh 19). As for the tribe of Levi, it had no portion in a particular region of the Promised Land, but only some scattered cities, because it was consecrated to service (Num 18:20, 35:1-8).

Judah: his name means praise. His father prophesies to him that his brothers will glorify him and give thanks to him, and that he will be strong and will strike his enemies on the back of the neck, that is, they will flee before him, and his brothers will bow down to him, because from him comes David the prophet, and his descendants are the kings of the kingdom of Judah; and then from his descendants comes also Christ, the King of kings, to whom the whole world bows down.
A lion's whelp: a cub, that is, the young son of the lion.
From the prey you have gone up: strong like the lion that devours its enemies and goes up victorious in wars.
He stooped down, he couched: he settled after his victory.
Who shall rouse him up: no one can disturb him or move him from his rest.

He likens him to the lion, the king of the beasts, in his strength and his victory over all his enemies, and then he settles, and everyone fears him and keeps away from him. And from the descendants of Judah comes Christ, who is victorious over Satan and binds him when He stoops down and couches on the cross, and no one can stop His redemption, His death and His resurrection. No one can raise Christ up, but it is He who raises Himself on the third day.
Sceptre: a golden rod that kings hold as a declaration of their reign.
Lawgiver: the one who decides laws and commandments.
From between his feet: from his descendants.
Shiloh: it means the One to whom everything belongs, or the Peacemaker, or the Savior.
Peoples: the whole world.

He declares that from the tribe of Judah will come David the king, from whose descendants come the kings over Jerusalem, until we reach Christ the Savior, who is Shiloh, and who reigns over the hearts of those who believe in Him from all the peoples of the world, and not only the believers from among the Jews.
The vine: that is, the grapevine or the vine tree.
The blood of grapes: the juice of the grape that becomes wine.
Darker in the eyes from wine: a figure for much drinking of wine, so that the eyes sparkle and are able to see sharply.
Whiter in the teeth from milk: a figure for the abundance of milk and of the flocks that yield it, which symbolizes the words of Christ, who comes from his descendants, and which nourish like milk.

He prophesies to him the many good things, symbolized by the abundance of vines and the grape juice that comes from them, and by the many flocks that yield milk: the land will be fertile and he will possess many flocks. This also symbolizes the blood of Christ the Redeemer, which we receive in the Church in the sacrament of Holy Communion.

When God gives you material blessings, take care to thank Him and to lift your eyes to the greater spiritual blessings in the Kingdom of Heaven, so that you are not absorbed in material things, but they lift you up to the love of God and to clinging to Him.
The haven of the sea: the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, west of the Jordan River.
A haven of ships: that is, the ports.

His border shall be unto Zidon: it reaches the city of Sidon, which lies on the Mediterranean about 25 miles south of present-day Beirut. Jacob prophesied that Zebulun would dwell on the coast of the Mediterranean and work in trade and mix with the nations, and that this would expose him to the worship of idols and to imitating their corruption; but when he believes in Christ, who preached in this region, he becomes a light to the world and a preacher of Christ (Mt 4:15, 16).
Shall judge his people: shall rule himself.
Dan is the first son of a maidservant, for he is the son of Bilhah the maidservant, but he is counted as a tribe like the rest of the tribes, ruling himself.
A serpent: the male snake.
In the way .. in the path: he pursues his enemies with cunning and is victorious over them.
That biteth the horse heels, so that his rider shall fall backward: with shrewdness he strips the enemy of his weapons and his strength and so triumphs over him.

He likened Dan to the serpent because he was characterized by cunning and shrewdness. He was not distinguished by the great number of his soldiers or by military strength, but he won by shrewdness combined with courage.
When he likened him to the serpent, he remembered Satan, the first serpent, and longed for the Messiah the Savior.
When afflictions come upon you or you fall into various sins, do not despair, but rise and ask for God's help, and if the affliction lasts long, wait for God's salvation, for He will never leave you.
A troop shall overcome him: enemies attack him.

He shall overcome at the last: he pursues his enemies after they have withdrawn from him and is victorious over them in the end. The tribe of Gad lived east of the Jordan, so it was exposed to many attacks by the Ammonites and the Amorites, who would overcome it, but it would return, pursue them and defeat them, and take much spoil from them.
His bread shall be fat: his good things are many.
Royal dainties: the precious goods that kings and great men seek.

Asher dwelt in a fertile land on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, in which olive trees were plentiful, so he obtained abundant harvests, from which he exported to the rest of the tribes. And because he lived beside the sea, he worked in trade, exporting and trading in the precious goods that the great men of the whole world seek. Moses the prophet also prophesied about him that he would dip his foot in oil because of the abundance of olive trees (Deut 33:24).
A hind: the female of the deer, a kind of gazelle that is very swift in movement.
Let loose: free and unbound.
Goodly words: his dealings are good and he is understanding.

He likens him to the female gazelle, swift in movement and unbound, because his land was fertile and he went out freely to work in it and enjoy prosperity; but in danger he would hasten to fight the enemies, and his dealings were good with the rest of the tribes around him.
Take care to speak well and to be kind in dealing with those around you, so that you build good relationships with them and live in peace, and are able to influence them and draw them to Christ.

He describes his beloved son Joseph as a fruitful branch from his father's tree: if his father had many descendants, he too would be fruitful. He is ever green and full of life because he is by a well of water, that is, spiritual and material blessings continue for him, as do loftiness and exaltation, since he became ruler over Egypt.
Have sorely grieved him: they persecuted him and afflicted him with bitterness, that is, distress.
The archers: those who were hostile to him, such as his brothers, or Potiphar's wife, or Potiphar himself, who cast him into prison.
Joseph was exposed to many persecutions from those around him.
The mighty God of Jacob: the beloved and strong God.
From thence: from heaven.
The shepherd: the guide and leader.
The stone of Israel: the strong helper of Israel.

Joseph was able to stand firm by the help of Almighty God, who supports him from heaven, shepherds him and gives him success. So he stood firm in a pure life with God and was strengthened, and did not submit to sin, but passed successfully through all afflictions and became ruler over all Egypt, and even managed its affairs with wisdom and skill.
Blessings of heaven: the rains and the dew.
Blessings of the deep that lieth under: the rivers that water his land.

Of the breasts and of the womb: abundance of offspring and their strength, because he is nourished much from the breasts, that is, material blessings. He prophesied and asked for him God's blessings from heaven in the rains, and from the earth in the rivers, and abundance of offspring and their strength. The strength of the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh appeared in (Deut 33:13-17, Josh 17:17, 18).
Utmost: the summit of what a person desires and longs for.
Hills: the high places.
Everlasting: existing from of old, that is, from a long time ago. The meaning is that he receives blessings to the utmost of what he desires.
Separate from his brethren: set apart and distinguished from his brothers by his righteousness.

He told him that the blessings that would come upon him were greater than the blessings that his father and his grandfather had received, and that they would be to the utmost possible, because of his distinction and his righteousness.

Hold fast to your faith even if some wrong you and you endure afflictions through no fault of your own; stand firm in your principles and God will support you, and in the end you will receive inexpressible blessings that satisfy you on earth, and then you will enjoy them forever.

He describes him as courageous like the wolf that devours the spoil in the morning, and then, when it settles in the evening, he and his children eat of the prey as he divides it among them. It is said of his warriors and their mastery of war that they "could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss" (Judg 20:16). Thus Jacob prophesied to his sons, showing their various characteristics and warning them so that they would repent of their sins and walk uprightly. These are prophecies and teachings for all believers, so that they may guard against the devil's snares and hold fast to the virtues. His teachings and directions can be summarized as follows:
1- Reuben: guard against pride and lust.
2- Simeon and Levi: guard against plots, anger and vengeance.
3- Zebulun: guard against mixing with the wicked, and turn instead to preaching to them.
4- Issachar: he calls him to endurance and perseverance.
5- Dan: he warns him against craftiness and cunning.
6- Gad: he calls him to hope in the struggle and not to despair.
7- Asher: he wishes him abundant blessings.
8- Naphtali: he praises him for his good relationships and his understanding with others.
9- Joseph: he wishes him continual growth.
10- Benjamin: he praises his courage.
Tribes: clans.
The preceding blessings are those with which Jacob blessed his sons, who became the heads of the tribes of the children of Israel.

He asked all his sons, as he had asked Joseph before in (ch. 47:29-31), to bury him in Canaan, in the cave of Machpelah, which is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, where Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah were buried.
